item.title: Day 1
item.description:
Day 1 #

Application Requirements #

Let’s get started and build a working application with agile development. This time, we will build a task management app as a simple example. It is hard to say what exactly makes a hands-on exercise like this “agile development,” but we will proceed without doing a rigid design up front, adding the features we need as we go. Read on as if a new Story that adds a feature is added at each step.

item.title: Facilitation
item.description:
Facilitation #

Overview #

Facilitation means helping conferences and meetings (MTGs) run smoothly. The person who takes on the role of facilitation is called the “facilitator.”

The Facilitator’s Role #

  • Create a place where everyone can share opinions with peace of mind
    • If some people stay silent, there may be an atmosphere that makes it hard to speak.
  • Define pointA and pointB
    • Clearly put the following two points into words and define them.
      • pointA: The current situation before the MTG
      • pointB: The ideal situation after the MTG
    The current situation is ***.
By the end, we want to ***.
  • Guide participants to pointB within the time
    • Based on experience, estimate how much time should be allotted, and make an effort to finish within that time.
      If you are unsure because of limited experience, consult with the MTG members and decide together.
      • It is desirable to reach the goal efficiently, but the path does not have to be a straight line.
      • The facilitator is there to correct the course, not to make decisions or reach conclusions.

Why Facilitation? #

In team activities, team members hold discussions and make decisions, so the role of a facilitator who keeps MTGs running smoothly is important. Even when it is not an MTG, decide on a facilitator whenever several people are talking.

item.title: Getting Started with Software Testing
item.description:
Getting Started with Software Testing #

So far we have learned about agile, Scrum, and XP. Since each of those was about mindsets and frameworks, many of you are probably wondering, “So how exactly do we actually develop software?”

Don’t worry: the main part of this document starts here!

In this chapter we will talk about software testing, but unlike the previous chapters, it is designed as a hands-on chapter where you learn by doing. Please get your favorite IDE or text editor ready as you read this chapter.

item.title: How Our Team Works
item.description:
How Our Team Works #

We aim for development at a sustainable pace in a team with psychological safety.

  • Pair work
    • All work is done in pairs.
    • This helps prevent rework, share information, transfer skills, and more.
  • Focus
    • Members are dedicated 100% to the project. (Including members from the client.)
    • Avoid side conversations during meetings.
    • Snacks and drinks are provided in the office for everyone to use freely. (Going out to buy them is a waste of time.)
  • Flat
    • All members maintain flat relationships (no leader) and call each other by nicknames.
    • Respect each individual and create opportunities for everyone to speak.
    • The team handles everything together, both good and bad.
  • Timeboxing
    • Work with an awareness of time and a good rhythm.
    • If a discussion drags on, consider splitting the topic.
    • When a discussion gets stuck, think about what would be needed to make a decision.
  • Don’t accumulate fatigue
    • Take a break of about 5–10 minutes every hour.
    • Refresh with table tennis.
    • Strictly leave the office at 18:00.
  • Kaizen and growth
    • Hold a team retrospective every week.
    • Regularly set aside time for feedback in pairs.
    • Pay attention to the team’s health and address issues early.

Team Rhythm #

The team develops in one-week iterations. We set the development outlook at the IPM, check the daily situation at the daily standup, and hold a retrospective on Friday, continuing to improve so that we become an even better team the following week.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Introduction #

Agile development and in-house development have been talked about for quite some time now, and our company is no exception. However, unlike the traditional waterfall approach, agile development cannot be done in a one-size-fits-all way, and for that reason it has also been an area where knowledge has rarely been put into writing.

If things stay that way, knowledge becomes concentrated in a few individuals, and the organization cannot scale agile development. Experience is extremely important in agile development. It is essential to actually go through the development process, internalize it, and make it a habit. In the first place, you will not become able to do agile development just by taking a particular training course, nor will you become able to do it just by reading this guide.

item.title: Lean Startup Agile Flow
item.description:
Lean Startup Agile Flow #

In Lean Startup Agile, a “balanced team” practices the “Lean XP” development approach, continuously developing the product with agility while repeatedly validating hypotheses with users.

  • Lean XP
    • Through Lean Startup and user-centered design practices, repeatedly validate hypotheses with users and avoid building waste (= things users will not use)
    • Through Extreme Programming (XP) practices, build high-quality software that is resilient to change
  • Balanced team
    • Achieve true agility through the business side’s participation in development and flat, frequent collaboration among members

item.title: Manifesto for Agile Software Development
item.description:
Manifesto for Agile Software Development #

If we were to give a concise answer to the question of what agile development is, it would be: “Development that is grounded in the mindset of the Manifesto for Agile Software Development and follows the 12 Principles of Agile Development.” Let’s start by reading through the Manifesto for Agile Software Development .

Manifesto for Agile Software Development

We are uncovering better ways of developing
software by doing it and helping others do it.
Through this work we have come to value:

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan

That is, while there is value in the items on
the right, we value the items on the left more.

This manifesto was created in 2001 by well-known software developers such as Kent Beck and Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob). “Individuals and interactions over processes and tools,” “Working software over comprehensive documentation,” “Customer collaboration over contract negotiation,” and “Responding to change over following a plan”: these four are declared as the mindset that must be upheld in agile development.

item.title: Modernization Agile Flow
item.description:
Modernization Agile Flow #

In Modernization Agile, an existing legacy system that has become a black box is analyzed from a business perspective, and development proceeds starting with what is needed. As with Lean Startup Agile, a “balanced team” practices the “Lean XP” development approach.

After the project starts, analysis is carried out during the first 2–4 weeks, and actual development begins in weeks 3–5.

When business processes are revisited along with the modernization, as in “Lean Startup Agile,” the team understands users and validates ideas through research, and proceeds with development in order of priority alongside the current business processes.

item.title: Office Standup
item.description:
Office Standup #

Overview #

A meeting held standing up, in which all the teams working in the same workplace gather. The following are shared:

  • NewFaces (new members)
  • Interestings (things that are interesting or of interest)
  • Helps (things you are struggling with or want help with)
  • Events (today’s events)

Purpose #

Create a daily work rhythm together with the members working in the same workplace. It also provides an opportunity for communication beyond team boundaries.

item.title: ONEbase Values
item.description:
ONEbase Values #

Core Values #

3 Things to Make it Work / 3 Agreements #

3 Things to Make it Work # 

1. Trust in team & process
2. Interest in users
3. Willingness to be wrong

3 Agreements # 

1. Decisions today are what we start woth tomorrow
2. We're not supposed to get it right today, just get close
3. Our confidence in decisions are based on current understanding

item.title: Persona
item.description:
Persona #

Overview #

A persona is a prototype model of a user. Research such as interviews is conducted with many real users, and similar needs, goals, contexts, and tasks are collected to create the persona. When information is lacking, a persona is created based on hypotheses (a proto-persona), and its content is updated after validation.

The following are visualized as part of a persona:

  • User name (the persona’s name) and an illustration
  • Facts (e.g., industry, experience, job title)
  • Behaviors & Habits (e.g., actions, routines, likes and dislikes)
  • Needs & Goals (e.g., wants to do ~, aims for ~)

item.title: Product Roadmap
item.description:
Product Roadmap #

Overview #

A product roadmap clarifies the path (strategy) for realizing the product vision. It consists of a series of goals that help development move toward the product vision, and shows the expected way the product will evolve over time.

A product roadmap organizes content such as the following across multiple time horizons (now, near future, far future):

  • Outcomes
  • Problems to solve
  • Success metrics

Example time horizons

  • Now, 3 months later (start of user testing), 7 months later (start of production operation)
  • Now, 1 month later, 4 months later (planned to match budget allocation in 3-month units)

item.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
item.description:
The Single Responsibility Principle #

What Is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)? #

The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that there should never be more than one reason for a class to change.

For example, consider the design shown below.

classDiagram
Computational Geometry Application --> Rectangle
Graphical Application --> Rectangle
Graphical Application --> GUI
Rectangle --> GUI
class Rectangle {
 +void draw()
 +double area()
}

The Rectangle class has two methods: one draws a rectangle on the screen, and the other calculates the area of the rectangle. Here, two applications use the Rectangle class.

item.title: Software Design for Agile Development
item.description:
Software Design for Agile Development #

In agile development, the required software specifications keep changing throughout development. That is why we need a “flexible” design that is resilient to change.

To be able to design and implement flexibly in a way that is resilient to change, it is extremely important to know the principles of object-oriented programming, such as the SOLID principles and design patterns, and to be able to put them to use.

item.title: TDD
item.description:
TDD #

Overview #

Test-driven development (TDD) is a development technique that repeats the process of writing a test first, then implementing the feature, and then refactoring the code.
See also Test-First Development and What Is Test-Driven Development .

Why TDD? #

As development progresses, the number of features implemented in the product gradually increases and the source code becomes more complex, so development speed can be expected to slow down.
For continuous development, it is desirable to always be able to keep developing at a fast pace.

item.title: What Is a Designer
item.description:
What Is a Designer #

Designers deliver value in the form of design decisions. Their job is to deeply understand users in order to define solutions that are desirable and easy to use for them. Working with the Product Manager, they validate assumptions about users and solutions in combination with user research.

Within a balanced team, they contribute to the product’s success by bringing the perspective of Desirable (user value) through user-centered design methodologies.

item.title: What Is a Developer
item.description:
What Is a Developer #

Developers (Devs) are responsible for implementing the backlog and building the product. They also give input on technical aspects when solutions are being considered, playing a part in the team’s understanding and decision-making. The basic approach to development follows Twelve-Factor .

Within a balanced team, they contribute to the product’s success by bringing the perspective of Feasible (technical feasibility) through the Extreme Programming methodology.

item.title: What Is a Product Manager
item.description:
What Is a Product Manager #

The Product Manager (PdM) discovers products that create value for the company and users, and leads the team so that those products can be realized. They drive decision-making for releasing good features while involving the team. They need to clearly understand who the users are, what they need, what impact the product will have on the business, and who the stakeholders are. They also need to work closely with the team.

item.title: What is Extreme Programming
item.description:
What is Extreme Programming #

Extreme Programming (XP) is a more practical collection of practices for carrying out development within the agile framework, proposed by Kent Beck, one of the members who issued the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. Scrum defined meetings and artifacts, but it did not go as far as defining how to develop within that framework. XP’s practices complement Scrum by covering “how to develop,” which Scrum does not define.

item.title: What is Scrum
item.description:
What is Scrum #

Scrum is one of the agile development methods. It was formulated by Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber in the 1990s. Scrum has the following characteristics:

  • It maximizes outcomes by ordering requirements based on value, risk, and necessity, and building the product in that order
  • In Scrum, work proceeds in fixed, short periods of time. These fixed periods are called timeboxes
  • The current situation and problems are always made visible. This is called transparency
  • The team regularly checks its progress, whether the product being built is delivering the expected outcomes, and whether there are problems with how the work is being done. This is called inspection
  • If there are problems with the way of working, or if there is a better way to do things, the way of working itself is changed. This is called adaptation

Scrum only defines the events the development team should hold, the roles, and the artifacts it should create, and the team itself has to think about how to actually apply those rules. Scrum also does not specifically prescribe things needed to build a product, such as how to write code; the team has to figure those out for itself. For this reason, it can be said that Scrum is a framework for agile development.

item.title: What Is the Swift Method
item.description:
What Is the Swift Method #

Background #

When modernizing a legacy system, you face problems such as the following:

  • No one with knowledge of the legacy system remains
  • The languages and technologies are old and hard to understand
  • Source code comments, design documents, and the like have not been maintained
  • Technical debt from stopgap measures has piled up
  • It is unclear which features are important and what the priorities are
  • Requirements have changed

Because of these problems caused by the legacy system becoming a black box, maintenance, responding to new requirements, and impact analysis become difficult, and time ends up being spent analyzing documents, features, and programs that are not needed.

item.title: 12 Principles of Agile Development
item.description:
12 Principles of Agile Development #

What was declared in the Manifesto for Agile Software Development described the mindset that matters in agile development. Now let’s look at the 12 Principles of Agile Development that form its background. There is a link to them on the Manifesto for Agile Software Development page mentioned earlier.

Principles behind the Agile Manifesto


We follow these principles:
Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer
through early and continuous delivery
of valuable software.

Welcome changing requirements, even late in
development. Agile processes harness change for
the customer's competitive advantage.

Deliver working software frequently, from a
couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a
preference to the shorter timescale.

Business people and developers must work
together daily throughout the project.

Build projects around motivated individuals.
Give them the environment and support they need,
and trust them to get the job done.

The most efficient and effective method of
conveying information to and within a development
team is face-to-face conversation.

Working software is the primary measure of progress.

Agile processes promote sustainable development.
The sponsors, developers, and users should be able
to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.

Continuous attention to technical excellence
and good design enhances agility.

Simplicity--the art of maximizing the amount
of work not done--is essential.

The best architectures, requirements, and designs
emerge from self-organizing teams.

At regular intervals, the team reflects on how
to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts
its behavior accordingly.

Next, let’s interpret these principles.

item.title: Balanced Team
item.description:
Balanced Team #

Three Roles #

A balanced team is formed of three roles (Product Manager/Designer/Developer), each responsible for business value, user value, and technical feasibility respectively. This enables quick and correct decisions and leads the product to success. Every one of these perspectives is essential to the success of a product, and it is important that the roles provide information to one another and respect each perspective’s thinking. To this end, the team is kept small, works together in the same place, and members always communicate proactively with one another in flat relationships.

item.title: CI/CD
item.description:
CI/CD #

Overview #

CI/CD is a practice that combines continuous integration (CI) and continuous delivery (CD). Automating build, test, and deployment makes them repeatable.

Why CI/CD? #

Introducing CI/CD lets you detect bugs and carry out release work efficiently. In addition, because tests can be run automatically, it is an essential practice for agile development, in which development is carried out iteratively.

What happens without CI/CD? #

  • Repeated testing piles up, and you cannot invest in adding features
  • Conflicts occur frequently when merging
  • Settings specific to the production environment get overlooked
  • Integration with external systems fails, or integration performance degrades

Benefits of CI/CD #

  • Bugs can be detected and release work carried out efficiently
  • Software can always be kept in a working state
  • Risks from releases can be found early

Key Points of CI/CD #

Divide into stages with the testing strategy in mind #

Developers want to run comprehensive tests in the CI/CD environment to gain greater confidence in quality, but comprehensive tests take a fair amount of time to provide feedback. To solve this problem, a deployment pipeline is usually divided into several stages. The earlier stages flush out most problems and provide quick feedback. The later stages take their time running comprehensive tests to raise the quality of the product. An example of dividing a deployment pipeline into stages is shown below.

Event Storming #

It is an activity for visualizing the “current state” and the “ideal state” of an existing system so that the whole team shares a common understanding. item.title: Extreme Programming Practices
item.description:
Extreme Programming Practices #

Customer as a team member #

It is desirable for the customer and developers to work closely together, sitting face to face in the same space. Working in the same space lets each side understand the other’s problems and work together toward solving them. This literally refers to physical distance: it is most ideal for the customer and developers to work in the same room. The greater the distance, the harder it becomes to truly incorporate the customer into the team.

item.title: MVP
item.description:
MVP #

Overview #

An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is the minimum product that can deliver value to users. It is used in the hypothesis validation process.

  • Minimum: built with minimal time and investment
  • Viable: provides an experience sufficient to show value to users and validate hypotheses

Why MVP? #

An MVP is used to validate the biggest hypotheses at minimal cost and minimize the biggest risks.
Having users use the product early and getting feedback helps you decide whether to keep building the product and whether to continue it as a business. By validating hypotheses at minimal cost, you lose little even if a hypothesis turns out to be wrong and you decide not to continue the business.
Also, even as part of the hypothesis validation process, delivering the product to users early raises awareness and gives you an advantage over competitors.

item.title: OKRs
item.description:
OKRs #

Overview #

OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) are a goal management method.
They link the team’s goals (Objectives) with the results needed to achieve them (Key Results), and the team frequently checks progress on the OKRs and gives feedback.

  • Step 1: Set the Objectives
    • Set the goals
  • Step 2: Set the Key Results
    • Set the results needed to achieve the goals
  • Step 3: Share the OKRs within the team
    • Keep the content of the OKRs open (create a Miro board for progress tracking, etc.)
  • Step 4: Regular feedback
    • Until the goals are achieved, frequently check progress and give feedback
      • Have each member rate the degree of achievement for the Key Results
        • The team decides on the rating breakdown
      • If they are not achieved, analyze the cause and identify the necessary action items

Why OKRs? #

They are effective for clarifying work priorities and achieving goals efficiently. By clarifying the work needed to achieve the goals, it becomes easier to see which tasks to focus on. They also clarify the actions members should take toward the team’s goals, so everyone can get on the same page.

item.title: Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
item.description:
The Open Closed Principle #

What Is the Open-Closed Principle (OCP)? #

The Open-Closed Principle (OCP) states that software entities (classes, modules, functions, etc.) should be open for extension but closed for modification.

With a “rigid” design, even a small change to a program affects every module that depends on the changed part. Applying the Open-Closed Principle lets you keep the impact of such modifications small.

item.title: Psychological Safety
item.description:
Psychological Safety #

Ensuring “psychological safety” is extremely important in carrying out a project. “Psychological safety” refers to a state in which team members can speak and act with peace of mind, without being rejected or punished for voicing ideas, questions, concerns, mistakes, and so on. If a high level of “psychological safety” can be maintained, the following benefits can be gained.

  • Communication becomes more active and team performance improves
  • A positive mindset forms and improvement activities become more active
  • People become more willing to take an interest in what is around them, creating more opportunities for growth

item.title: Roles
item.description:
Roles #

Scrum defines three roles in an agile development team:

  • Product owner
  • Product development team
  • Scrum master

Let’s look at each of them.

Product owner #

The product owner is the person responsible for the product. They are also the manager of the product backlog, which is described later. The product owner is responsible for maximizing the value the product creates by making use of the product development team. For this reason, in addition to managing the product backlog, they take on roles such as the following:

item.title: Scenario
item.description:
Scenario #

Overview #

A scenario is a concrete, chronological description of how target users go about using the software.

Scenarios are created as follows:

  • Write the most basic scenario (the happy path)
    • Rare cases and error cases are not needed at first
  • Write with the start and end points of the work in mind
    • What triggers the scenario to start (before use)
    • What counts as reaching the goal, and what happens afterward (after use)
  • Write with the people involved and the touchpoints (things and information) in the scenario in mind
  • Write concisely so the flow is clear
  • Write so that the persona’s feelings come across
  • Sometimes both a current (“Current”) and a future (“Future”) scenario are written

Key Points of Scenarios #

  • There is no need to write detailed UI behavior
    • Not good:
      When Takeshi enters a user name in the search field, an incremental search runs and narrows down the candidates. He selects the target user and selects the “Edit” button. A pop-up screen then appears, and he edits the information.
    • Good:
      Takeshi narrows down the target users and edits their information.
  • Writing scenarios can make you notice new assumptions, areas you don’t know about, and the persona’s needs
  • As with personas, revise them as needed whenever you notice new facts or mistakes

item.title: Structure and Roles
item.description:
Structure and Roles #

Core Team #

Product Managers #

Product Managers (PdMs) are responsible for building the right thing: they prioritize features based on business value, user value, and technical difficulty, and deliver a valuable product. They write user stories to share information accurately within the team, and after development is complete, they perform acceptance checks to confirm that the product delivers value as intended. In addition to communication within the Core team, PdMs hold CL meetings and Inception/Outception sessions to coordinate information with the PMO and other teams. Because they have a grasp of a wide range of information, PdMs often take the lead in facilitating meetings overall (things go more smoothly when the person who understands the big picture facilitates).

item.title: Structure and Roles
item.description:
Structure and Roles #

Core Team #

Product Managers #

Product Managers (PdMs) are responsible for building the right thing: they prioritize features based on business value, user value, and technical difficulty, and deliver a valuable product. They write user stories to share information accurately within the team, and after development is complete, they perform acceptance checks to confirm that the product delivers value as intended. In addition to communication within the Core team, PdMs hold CL meetings and Inception/Outception sessions to coordinate information between the Core team and Stakeholders/Informed. Because they have a grasp of a wide range of information, PdMs often take the lead in facilitating meetings overall (things go more smoothly when the person who understands the big picture facilitates). Also, when no Designer is involved, they need to provide the information Devs need to implement design stories, for example by creating mockups.

item.title: Team Standup
item.description:
Team Standup #

Overview #

A meeting held standing up with all members of the team. The following are shared, and tasks are checked.

  • What I did yesterday
  • What I will do today
  • Learnings / things I am struggling with

Purpose #

Share the plans and progress of every team member’s tasks, detect issues early, and help one another as a team to move forward.

item.title: Warming Up
item.description:
Warming Up #

Here, let’s try building an extremely simple console application using test-driven development. We use Java as the development language here, but all of the exercises below are based on well-known problems, so feel free to try them in your favorite language.

What Is Test-Driven Development? #

Before we get into practice, let’s review test-driven development. Test-driven development is, literally, a development process in which you first implement code that tests the product’s behavior, and then implement the product.

item.title: Artifacts
item.description:
Artifacts #

The Scrum Guide defines three artifacts that the Scrum team should create:

  • Product backlog
  • Sprint backlog
  • Increment

Let’s look at each of them.

Product backlog #

The product backlog is an ordered list of everything the product needs, such as the features, requirements, requests, and fixes you want to realize.

Let’s look at a concrete example. This is the actual product backlog of a project the author is assigned to.

item.title: Boris
item.description:
Boris #

Overview #

Boris is one of the activities used when you want to break down an existing system into several smaller services. By having the team identify and discuss the connections (communication methods and data) between service candidates (the output of Event Storming), the team can build a shared understanding of the relationships between services. It is the second activity in the overall Swift Method.

item.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
item.description:
The Liskov Substitution Principle #

What Is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)? #

The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. What happens if we do not follow this principle?

Suppose a function f takes as its argument a pointer or reference to some base class B. Now imagine there is a class D derived from B, and passing it to f in place of B causes f to misbehave. In that case, we say that class D violates the Liskov Substitution Principle.

item.title: Pair Programming
item.description:
Pair Programming #

Overview #

Pair programming is a technique in which developers program in pairs. Code is written by a pair consisting of a driver and a navigator. The driver concentrates on writing code, while the navigator keeps the design in mind and shows the driver the way forward or gives advice.

Why Pair Programming? #

By working in pairs and teaching each other, knowledge sharing among developers advances and overall skills improve. Always working with two pairs of eyes and two minds helps ensure quality. Working together with someone also helps maintain work efficiency: you can keep working without slacking off more than when working alone, and for some people it becomes a source of motivation.

item.title: Pre-IPM
item.description:
Pre-IPM #

Overview #

Pre-IPM is a meeting in which draft user stories are reviewed from the Developer’s perspective in preparation for the IPM (Iteration Planning Meeting). It is held by the Product Manager, the Designer, and one pair of Developers.

Purpose #

Confirm that the user stories are sufficiently prepared for discussion and estimation at the IPM and for starting implementation.

Frequency and Timing #

  • Once a week, 30–60 minutes
  • Held regularly on a fixed day of the week to keep the team’s rhythm
  • If there are only a few target user stories, or they are unlikely to be revised based on Developer feedback, Pre-IPM and IPM are held together

How to Run It #

  • The Product Manager and Designer explain the user stories to be estimated at the IPM
  • The Developers review the user stories from the following perspectives
    • Is it expressed in a way that makes the value to the user understandable?
    • Is it feasible?
    • Is the story an appropriate size (does it need to be split)?
    • Is a SPIKE or investigation needed before implementing the user story?
  • If changes are needed, agree on how to revise them
  • (After the meeting) The Product Manager/Designer revise the user stories

Tips

  • Which Developers attend is decided based on skills, the type of user story, the status of ongoing work, and so on.

item.title: Product Vision / Value Proposition
item.description:
Product Vision / Value Proposition #

Overview #

The product vision defines the world you are trying to realize through the product. Project members always keep this vision in mind as they make day-to-day decisions.

The value proposition concretely describes the value provided to users. It clarifies what pains currently exist and how the product can solve those problems.

Key Points of a Product Vision #

  • A product vision should convey the following

item.title: Research Planning
item.description:
Research Planning #

Overview #

In research planning, you plan the hypotheses to validate in the next user research and how to validate them.

Preparation proceeds in the following steps:

  1. Set the research theme (question)
  2. List high-priority risks and assumptions
  3. Turn them into testable hypotheses
  4. Make the validation methods concrete
  5. Organize the tasks and preparation needed to carry it out

Key Points of Research Planning #

  • Writing down risks is the starting point
  • Risks depend on the members’ assumptions
  • Think about risks and assumptions on a regular basis
  • Research planning is difficult, but you get a feel for it as you do it more often

Research planning example

item.title: Summary
item.description:
Summary #

We have now read through the Manifesto for Agile Software Development and the 12 Principles of Agile Development. In fact, not a single concrete development method has appeared so far. Everything has been about mindset.

You might be thinking, “Don’t tell me about mindset, tell me about concrete development methods.” However, in agile, this mindset matters even more than development methods. As you can see from what you have read so far, agile does not prescribe any concrete development methods in the first place. This is a decisive difference from waterfall, so many people may find it confusing. Agile is a development model premised on embracing all kinds of change. It is best to think of it as taking this form because rigidly prescribing even the development methods would make it hard to respond to change.

item.title: Summary
item.description:
Summary #

Extreme Programming (XP) is an agile development process built from a simple and concrete set of practices. This development process is used by many teams and has achieved substantial results.

XP is a highly versatile software development method, and it should be possible to adopt it in many development projects. And it is essential for each development team to add and change practices through retros, shaping a set of practices that better suits the team.

item.title: User Story Mapping
item.description:
User Story Mapping #

Overview #

In user story mapping, you extract user stories while mapping them by user actions (horizontal axis) and priority (vertical axis) to organize the user stories.

  1. Write out the actions each user (persona) takes when using the product

  2. Write out the detailed requirements (user stories) needed for each action

    Example perspectives for extracting user stories

    • Items that can be seen on the screen
    • Operations performed on the screen
    • Input fields specified on the screen
    • The order in which items are displayed on the screen

  3. Map each user story by priority

    Example perspectives for priority

    • must have (a problem without it)
    • good to have (better to have)
    • nice to have (makes the UX even more effective if present)
    • edge case

    Example releases resulting from prioritization (user payments)

    • Release 1: Credit card payments only
    • Release 2: Add cashless payments such as PayPay

item.title: XP Values
item.description:
XP Values #

XP is based on five values.

  • Communication

    Everyone on the team works together at every stage of the project.

  • Simplicity

    Developers strive to save time and effort by writing simple code that brings value to the product.

  • Feedback

    Team members deliver software frequently, get feedback on it, and improve the product in response to new requirements.

  • Courage

    Without making excuses, evaluate your own results objectively and respond to change.

  • Respect

    Everyone involved in the project contributes toward a common goal.

item.title: Day 4
item.description:
Day 4 #

By the end of Day 3, we were able to connect the frontend built with React to the backend built with Spring Boot. However, although we can display tasks, there is still no feature for adding tasks. From Day 4 on, let’s keep adding features.

Building the Add Task Screen #

Right now, the Client application does not have a router yet. For example, accessing http://localhost:5173/ shows the Home screen, and accessing http://localhost:5173/hogehoge also shows the Home screen.

item.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
item.description:
The Dependency Inversion Principle #

What Is the Dependency Inversion Principle? #

The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) states that

  • High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on “abstractions”.
  • “Abstractions” should not depend on implementation details. Implementation details should depend on “abstractions”.

It is very common in traditional software development for high-level modules to depend on low-level modules. Take the common three-tier web architecture as an example: the Controller class depends on the Service class, and the Service class depends on the Repository class.

item.title: Events
item.description:
Events #

Image source: アジャイル開発とは（中編）(What is Agile Development? Part 2)

Fujitsu’s public website happens to have a diagram explaining the Scrum process, so I will use it to explain.

Sprint #

In Scrum, development is carried out repeatedly in fixed periods ranging from one week up to a maximum of one month. This fixed period is called a sprint (sometimes also called an iteration). Within each period, the development team does all the work needed to complete product backlog items, such as planning, design, development, and testing.

item.title: How to Adopt Practices
item.description:
How to Adopt Practices #

Practices (methods and tools) are only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath the visible iceberg lie Principles and Values. Rather than superficially imitating and using Practices, it is important to learn with an awareness of the Principles and Values on which they are based.

item.title: IPM
item.description:
IPM #

Overview #

The IPM (Iteration Planning Meeting) is a meeting in which we estimate each user story and plan the next iteration. The Product Manager leads the meeting, the Product Manager and Designer explain the value to be delivered, and all the Developers estimate together.

Purpose #

We share the content of the prioritized user stories so that the Developers can proceed with implementation. We also estimate the stories to forecast how many user stories can be completed in the iteration one to two weeks ahead.

item.title: Prototyping
item.description:
Prototyping #

Overview #

In prototyping, the UI of the software is designed.

The work proceeds as follows:

  • Following the scenario, consider the screen transitions and the layout of each screen
    • You may also organize the requirements to be met, and have each person make rough sketches and share them.
  • Once the rough overall picture is ready, create the UI with a tool
  • Share with the Product Manager and Developers as appropriate

Key Points of Prototyping #

  • Even before the layout has been fine-tuned, research can be done using it as a prototype. Once you confirm there are no problems, you can refine it for development
  • Build it in stages according to the hypotheses you want to validate and the iteration schedule. Don’t build all the screens at once
  • Use a tool that makes it easy to collaborate with Developers and change course (we use Figma)
  • Prepare a style guide (colors, typography), etc.
  • As much as possible, turn things into shared parts (components) from the start, aiming for a build that is resilient to change
  • UI design skills are not acquired overnight

Script Creation

item.title: SnapE
item.description:
SnapE #

Overview #

SnapE is one of the activities used when you want to break down an existing system into several smaller services. By having the team identify and discuss the contents of service candidates (the output of Event Storming)—how they communicate, the data they own, stories, risks, and so on—the team can build a shared understanding of the contents of each service. It is the third activity in the overall Swift Method.

item.title: Solo Programming
item.description:
Solo Programming #

Overview #

Solo programming is a technique in which a developer programs alone. It has been adopted at many SI (system integration) sites, where developers quietly carry out design, development, and testing on their own.

Why Solo Programming? #

In projects with characteristics like the following, short-term development speed may have to take priority over development sustainability.

  • The project deadline must be strictly met
  • The product requirements cannot be changed

With solo programming, the number of tasks the team can work on at the same time increases compared with pair programming. Developers can also turn their own ideas into code without discussing them with others. As a result, faster development becomes possible, albeit temporarily.

item.title: Team Building
item.description:
Team Building #

Team building is an effort to create a team that pulls together toward achieving its purpose and goals, with each member proactively making the most of their abilities.
Team building brings the following benefits.

  • More active communication
  • Higher member motivation
  • Better team performance
  • Fostering of the right mindset

The following activities are effective for team building.

Retrospective

Feedback

Ice Break

Team Health Check

1on1

Radio Taiso

item.title: Test Doubles
item.description:
Test Doubles #

Now that you understand the flow of test-driven development, let’s next learn about testing with test doubles.

What Is a Test Double? #

There are very few cases where the class or method under test does not depend on any other class. The classes it depends on, in turn, depend on other classes.

Because software works through many classes depending on each other, guaranteeing the behavior of the software as a whole is more valuable than guaranteeing the behavior of a single class. On the other hand, it is a major drawback that a unit test may fail because of a problem outside the class under test.

item.title: User Story
item.description:
User Story #

Overview #

A user story expresses a user’s requirement (who wants to do what, and for what purpose).
In a user story, the user’s requirement is written in the following format:

As [user (persona)]
I want [what the user wants to do]
So that [the resulting outcome]

In addition, the criteria for confirming that the user story has been achieved (Acceptance Criteria) are written in the following form:

2×2 #

Overview #

A 2×2 (two by two) is a technique for making decisions by rigorously prioritizing. By setting two decision-making perspectives on the vertical and horizontal axes and ordering items along each perspective, you can determine priorities: items in the upper-right of the four quadrants are “what to do now,” and items in the lower-left are “what you don’t need to do.”

Why 2×2? #

You can set priorities while balancing multiple competing perspectives as axes, which makes it easier to explain logically why a decision was made and easier to gain the understanding of everyone involved.

item.title: CL Meeting
item.description:
CL Meeting #

Overview #

The CL meeting is a forum for sharing information with the CL (Client Liaison)/PMO.

Purpose #

By sharing information regularly, we build a cooperative relationship aimed at the success of the project.

Frequency and Timing #

  • Once a week, 30 minutes
  • Held at the end of the week (Friday)

How to Run It #

  • Updates from the agile team
    • Development progress
      • Quantitative assessment (points of completed stories, velocity)
      • Qualitative assessment
    • Work status and upcoming plans for each role
    • Issues and requests
  • Updates from the PMO
    • PMO work status and upcoming plans
    • Issues and requests

Tips

item.title: Day 5
item.description:
Day 5 #

Now let’s create the backend API that creates a Todo.

Task Creation Backend API #

Tests #

First, let’s write a server test. We will write a test that sends a request to POST /todos with JSON set in the body and checks the response code and response data.

// TodoControllerTest.kt
package com.fujitsu.todoappserver.controller

import com.fasterxml.jackson.module.kotlin.jacksonObjectMapper
import com.fasterxml.jackson.module.kotlin.readValue
import com.fujitsu.todoappserver.model.Todo
import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat
import org.json.JSONObject
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.client.TestRestTemplate
import org.springframework.http.*

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class TodoControllerTest {
 @Autowired
 lateinit var restTemplate: TestRestTemplate

 @Test
 fun タスク一覧を取得できる() {
 val header = HttpHeaders()
 header.contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
 val response = restTemplate.exchange("/todos", HttpMethod.GET, HttpEntity(null, header), String::class.java)
 val mapper = jacksonObjectMapper()
 val articles: List<Todo> = mapper.readValue(response.body!!)
 assertThat(response.statusCode).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK)
 assertThat(articles.size).isEqualTo(0)
 }

 @Test
 fun タスクを新規作成できる() {
 val newTodoJson = JSONObject()
 newTodoJson.put("title", "test title")
 val header = HttpHeaders()
 header.contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
 val postResponse = restTemplate.exchange(
 "/todos",
 HttpMethod.POST,
 HttpEntity(newTodoJson.toString(), header),
 String::class.java
 )
 val mapper = jacksonObjectMapper()
 val todo: Todo = mapper.readValue(postResponse.body!!)
 assertThat(postResponse.statusCode).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED)
 assertThat(todo.id).isEqualTo(1)
 assertThat(todo.title).isEqualTo("test title")
 assertThat(todo.completed).isEqualTo(false)
 }
}

This is equivalent to the Get /Todos test we wrote the other day, so it should be fine.

item.title: E2E Testing
item.description:
E2E Testing #

What Is E2E Testing? #

So far we have looked at how to do unit testing and integration testing of software. However, we still don’t know whether the server and client work together properly so that the system behaves correctly. That is where E2E (End to End) testing comes in: a test that runs through the entire system. It is sometimes also called acceptance testing.

item.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
item.description:
The Interface Segregation Principle #

What Is the Interface Segregation Principle? #

The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) states that clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. This principle helps slim down “fat” interfaces. A class with a “fat” interface carries many interfaces, and those interfaces are only partially strongly related to each other. Looked at from another angle, this means that strongly related interfaces can be grouped together. Each group of member functions then serves a different client, because different clients need different member functions.

item.title: Remote Work
item.description:
Remote Work #

In remote work, the main means of communication is online. Because people do not see each other face to face when communicating online, the psychological distance between members grows and the barrier to small talk rises. Therefore, to communicate smoothly and build a team with high psychological safety, the following are needed.

  • Setting rules
  • Using effective tools
  • Running initiatives specific to remote work

Rules #

Rules for Team Meetings #

  • Mute yourself when you are not speaking
  • Turn your video on
  • If you leave or return during a session, let others know
  • As needed, use Zoom’s chat feature to ask to speak or to ask questions
  • Avoid side conversations, as they are distracting
  • Set clear goals and stick to the agenda schedule
  • Create an agenda on the fly as needed
  • Stay focused: put small talk and things you want to check later in the “parking lot,” and have side conversations at the appropriate time
  • Balance speaking time to improve collaboration and understanding

Tools #

Tuple #

  • Remote pair programming app

  • For macOS

item.title: Script Creation
item.description:
Script Creation #

Overview #

In script creation, you create a talk script that organizes the flow of the research session and the items to check.

Include the following:

  • Target users
  • The purpose of this research and the hypotheses to validate
    • Generative
    • Evaluative
    • Usability
  • Things to prepare
  • The script itself
    • What the interviewer says
    • Tasks to request / hypotheses to check
    • Items to check

Key Points of Script Creation #

  • Always do a rehearsal beforehand
    • Have someone play the interviewee
  • Don’t be particular about the format; adjust it so it is easy for the interviewer to talk

Conducting Research

item.title: Slices
item.description:
Slices #

Overview #

Slices is an activity for deciding where to start development. It is the fourth activity in the overall Swift Method.
The general flow of Slices is as follows:

  • Select business scenarios with high business value from Event Storming (selecting scenarios)
  • Add the elements needed to carry out the business to the scenarios (fleshing out the scenarios)
  • Link the services organized in Boris/SnapE to the flow (visualizing complexity/difficulty)
  • Decide the order of the scenarios (Slices) to develop based on business value and development complexity/difficulty (ordering when to start developing each scenario)

Participants #

Must #

  • People who write user stories
    Required, because user stories cannot be written without knowing the development priorities.
  • People who understand business priorities
    When deciding the order of development, the priority and certainty of the business need to be taken into account.

Option #

  • People who build things
    When deciding the order of development, taking difficulty and whether existing assets can be reused into account makes development easier to move forward.

Conditions for Moving On to the Next Activity #

  • Five scenarios have been listed as Slices and their order of development has been decided

How to Proceed #

  • Step 1: Select scenarios with high business value

    • Pick five scenarios with high business value from those identified in Event Storming
      • Because rework may occur, rather than prioritizing all scenarios, pick around five scenarios that are likely to be developed in the near term
      • When development progresses and it becomes necessary to start on the next scenario, add a new scenario (Slice) at that point

  • Step 2: Fill in the scenarios

    • Copy the picked scenarios for use as Slices
    • Go through the copied scenarios in order, and add the elements (events) needed to carry out the business to the scenario, or create new scenarios
      • For example, check and fill in from perspectives such as the following
        • Is a login operation needed?
        • How is that screen accessed?
        • What conditions are specified when searching on the screen?
        • What items are checked on the screen?
        • How is the data checked on the screen created?
      • Check that there is nothing that cannot be achieved when proceeding with development in order
      • It is enough if the team can share the information needed to decide the order of development, such as difficulty and dependencies (more specific details are checked when writing stories)
    • Link the services, UI, and external systems organized in Boris/SnapE to each event in the scenario
      • Things like needing multiple services or being related to external systems become visible, giving a sense of the complexity

item.title: Summary
item.description:
Summary #

So far, we have looked at Scrum’s roles, the artifacts a Scrum team should create, and the flow of development in a Scrum team. It is important that the product owner and the entire product development team understand what has been explained here.

In addition, to get good results with Scrum, you need to adopt and put into practice the five Scrum values.

  • Commitment
    • Each person commits to doing their utmost to achieve the goal
  • Courage
    • Have the courage to do the right thing and work on tough problems
  • Focus
    • Everyone focuses on the work of the sprint and on achieving the goal
  • Openness
    • Agree to be open about all the work and problems
  • Respect
    • Respect each other as capable individuals

It is important that the whole Scrum team not merely carry out the framework as written, but act based on these five values.

item.title: Conducting Research
item.description:
Conducting Research #

Overview #

In research, user interviews, user tests, and the like are conducted to obtain information for validating hypotheses.

The following work is carried out:

  • Conduct the research according to the script
  • The note-taker records what is said (in a Google spreadsheet)

Key Points of Conducting Research #

  • If you will share screens or record, get consent for that
  • Don’t jump straight into the main topic; keep in mind building a good relationship with the participant (rapport)
  • There is no need to be overly formal
  • When having participants try a prototype, tell them that it is the UI being evaluated, not the participants themselves
  • Don’t over-explain the UI. Observe how the participant operates it
  • Don’t lead the participant’s opinions
  • As a third party, you may dig into things that the client finds hard to ask. Striking the right balance is important
  • Research sessions last at most one hour
  • Tips for user testing are compiled in books on human-centered design, so read them

Synthesize

item.title: Day 6
item.description:
Day 6 #

Now that the client and server work together to create tasks, let’s write scenario tests.

Setting Up the E2E Test Environment #

First, let’s create an environment for E2E tests.

mkdir e2e
cd e2e
mkdir test
touch test/test.js 
npm init

When you run the npm init command, a setup dialog appears. For now, just press Enter for everything without setting anything, and create package.json. Then install testcafe, an E2E testing library.

item.title: Retrospective
item.description:
Retrospective #

Overview #

The retrospective (retro) is an activity in which the team reflects on its activities. Members openly bring up what went well and what did not go well in the iteration, and decide on actions for improvement. It is held in a relaxed atmosphere over drinks.

Purpose #

Its purpose is to continuously improve the team’s process, and it is an important activity in agile development. The team aligns its understanding so that good things are continued and things that do not go well are improved, leading to better team performance. In addition, a sense of unity emerges as the team shares together what went well and what they struggled with, and thinks about how to deal with it.

item.title: Tech Choice
item.description:
Tech Choice #

Overview #

Tech Choice is an activity in which the team discusses and decides which technologies to use before starting development. It is the fifth activity in the overall Swift Method. It is carried out after the priorities of the scenarios to start developing have been decided in Slices.

Participants #

Must #

  • People who build things
    Required, because the people who will actually build it afterward cannot build it unless they understand it.

Option #

  • People who decide the priority of user stories
    Required in order to understand the work needed during development (environment preparation, etc.).

Conditions for Moving On to the Next Activity #

  • The technologies to use have been decided

How to Proceed #

  • Select technologies such as the following
    • language
    • application framework
    • IDE
    • repository
    • Authentication & authorization
    • Cloud
    • Gateway
    • Container
    • Container Registory
    • Container Platform
    • DB
    • Queue

item.title: Sales Sync Meeting
item.description:
Sales Sync Meeting #

Overview #

The sales sync meeting is a forum for sharing information with the sales team and other people who serve as points of contact for each end user. When necessary, the team also asks the sales team for help, such as with research.

Purpose #

By sharing information regularly, we build a cooperative relationship aimed at the success of the project. People who serve as points of contact for end users need accurate information about the timing and content of product releases, as well as the direction of the product. Also, hearing the voices of end users, even on topics the team has not researched directly, can lead to new discoveries and become the seeds of the next hypotheses.

item.title: Synthesize
item.description:
Synthesize #

Overview #

In synthesis, you summarize from the research results whether the hypotheses were validated, whether there were new discoveries, and so on, and accumulate them as learnings.

Synthesis involves the following:

  • Put users’ remarks and behaviors on Post-it notes, organized by the items checked
  • Group the Post-it notes
  • Label what can be said from each group
    • What it means in a word
    • New needs
    • New insights (realizations)
  • Assign each hypothesis to one of “validated,” “wrong,” or “needs further validation”
  • Also compile the needs and insights

item.title: In Closing
item.description:
In Closing #

First of all, you have read this guide all the way to the end! Great work! You have taken the first step toward becoming an agile developer.

You may have thought, “If I understand this guide, doesn’t that make me an agile developer?” Unfortunately, that is not the case; this guide is only the first step toward becoming an agile developer. Nor do you become an agile developer by taking a particular training course or program.

item.title: Internal Sync
item.description:
Internal Sync #

Overview #

Internal Sync is a meeting held only among members from within the company. Members share what they learned from the day’s work, clear up open questions, and discuss future policies and ways of working.

Purpose #

When there are things that are hard to talk about in front of members from outside the company, this meeting provides psychological safety for sharing and consulting. It is also used as time to summarize learnings for internal reporting.

item.title: Recommended Books
item.description:
Recommended Books #

Here we recommend books that do not depend on any particular language or architecture.

The Art of Readable Code #

https://www.amazon.co.jp/dp/4873115655/

It hardly needs an introduction here, but it is a must-read for team development; joining product development without reading this book is like walking into someone else’s house with your shoes on.

It explains logically what readable code is. In agile development, we do not write documentation about the product (not only design documents, but also comments). Readable code itself becomes the documentation. Be sure to read it before joining product development so that you can write readable code.

item.title: Risks & Mitigations
item.description:
Risks & Mitigations #

Overview #

The team lists the risks to achieving its goals and considers measures to mitigate them. Each person’s assumptions are made visible, prioritized based on impact, the team’s state of learning, and so on, and then addressed.

Purpose #

Identifying risks and considering countermeasures helps improve the team’s performance. By validating the various assumptions made visible through this activity, the team can carry out its ideas with confidence and move forward.

item.title: Feedback
item.description:
Feedback #

Overview #

Give candid evaluations of and points for improvement on another person’s behavior.

  • Do it on a flat basis, regardless of seniority or position.
  • Always give feedback one-on-one.

What to Give Feedback On #

  • Tell the other person things that will benefit them.
  • Adapt the content to the situation.
    • Strengths / room for growth
    • What is going well / what would be good to change
    • What to start / what to stop / what to continue

The Mindset Behind Feedback # 

How can I personally become a better team member?
How can we work better together?

Purpose #

We encourage growth by building on each person’s strengths and improving their weaknesses. This also leads to building a better team.

item.title: Ice Break
item.description:
Ice Break #

Overview #

The team steps away from development work and plays games and the like together.

Purpose #

The aim is to stimulate communication among members and to refresh both mind and body.

Frequency and Timing #

  • About once every two weeks
  • Held so that it does not take a large chunk of time away from development
  • If the team agrees, it can be held at any time: during working hours, lunch breaks, short breaks, or after hours

How to Run It #

  • Decide what to do
  • Decide when to do it
  • Have fun

Examples

  • Table tennis
  • Switch
  • Word Wolf [How to play]
  • Various board games
  • Finding-things-in-common game [How to play]
  • GeoGuessr (a game of guessing locations in Street View) [How to play]
  • Small talk

item.title: Team Health Check
item.description:
Team Health Check #

Overview #

The team conducts an anonymous survey to make the state of the team visible.

Purpose #

The purpose is to learn how members feel by sharing opinions based on the survey results, take the actions the team needs, and make it a better team.

Frequency and Timing #

  • About once every two weeks
  • When there is a change in the project situation (structure, schedule, etc.)

How to Run It #

  • Step 1: Create the survey items (owner: Product Manager)
    • Set items such as the following
      • Psychological safety: I can freely say and share what I think. I also get feedback from the team
      • Vision: The vision for the business, service, and product is clear, and everyone on the team understands it
      • Mission: Everyone on the team shares what we should accomplish and the direction we should aim for
      • Autonomy: Rather than just doing what we are told, the team can make decisions to some extent
      • Enablement: Even after the engagement ends, we can teach other teams what we learned
      • Risk: We can work without fear of failure
      • Users: We understand the users’ needs
      • Stakeholders: They support the team and the product (they are interested in it)
      • Continuous improvement: We are always improving based on feedback from users
      • Attitude toward work: Working as a team is fun
    • Set up answer options such as the following
      • Answer choices
        • Going well, nothing to add
        • There are obstacles, but we can overcome them
        • There are problems that may negatively affect the team
      • Optional comment field (reason when choosing “there are obstacles” or “there are problems”)
  • Step 2: Answer the survey (owner: core members)
  • Step 3: Tally the survey responses (owner: Product Manager)
  • Step 4: Share the results (owner: core members)

    • Look at the survey results and exchange opinions within the team

    • If something is not going well for some reason, identify the necessary action items

    • Sample results

item.title: 1on1
item.description:
1on1 #

Overview #

Team members talk with each other one-on-one. Rather than a career-oriented 1on1 between a manager and a direct report, this is a casual conversation with a teammate you work closely with.

Purpose #

Through 1on1s, members share what went well and what they are worried about, ask for advice on their concerns, and offer new insights.

Frequency and Timing #

  • 1–2 times a month, about 15–30 minutes
  • Held as needed according to the wishes and circumstances of the members, without being bound by a fixed frequency

How to Run It #

  • Schedule it while taking into account pair assignments and the work in progress
  • Secure a place where you can talk one-on-one, such as Zoom or a meeting space
  • Hold the 1on1 meeting and clear your mind

    Example topics

    • Small talk
    • Thoughts about the team
    • Recent concerns
    • How you want to grow through the project

item.title: Radio Taiso
item.description:
Radio Taiso #

Overview #

Radio Taiso is a set of calisthenics performed to musical accompaniment, devised to improve physical fitness and maintain and promote health.
In Japan, it is widely loved by the public as an exercise that anyone can enjoy casually.

Purpose #

By moving our bodies and refreshing ourselves, we maintain the team’s concentration and the quality of our work.

  • Relieving stiff shoulders
  • Improving posture

Frequency and Timing #

  • Optional (e.g., every day after lunch break)

How to Run It #

  • The whole team does Radio Taiso together while playing a video on a site such as YouTube

References

  • Radio Taiso No. 1 (YouTube)
